For a while, the only thing Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) had in common was that they both made chips.

Nvidia rode the AI boom to become one of the world's most valuable companies, while Intel spent years trying to repair its business. Now they share a problem: shareholders who aren't sure what comes next. Nvidia released its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday, its first since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO, and the stock still fell the next day. Intel's slide deepened after it issued a weak outlook in late October.

Nvidia's revenue more than doubled year over year to $115.8 billion, and interim CEO Colette Kress raised the fiscal 2028 growth forecast to 75% from 70%. On the same call, though, board chair Harvey Jones said the board does not intend to reinstate Huang. That came only hours after Huang said he would be honored to return.

Nvidia stock now hovers near its lowest level since around June 2025. This week Intel was hit by a shareholder lawsuit and by a filing showing that Nvidia sold about a quarter of its Intel stake. Intel shares sit about 60% below their June peak.

So, where to now for these two embattled chip giants?

An investor going by the moniker of The Curious Analyst (TCA) has two very different reads on these stocks.

On Nvidia, TCA thinks the leadership drama is already reflected in the share price. The stock fell sharply when Huang stepped down, but the board's refusal to bring him back drew a much milder reaction. The investor takes that as a sign the market trusts Kress. In TCA's view, investors can now see what Nvidia looks like without its founder, and the danger of relying on one person has faded.

The business case rests on the product cycle. Vera Rubin added nearly $20 billion in revenue from the previous quarter, and the investor expects growth to hold up as it ramps alongside Blackwell Ultra. TCA also expects Nvidia to use up its remaining buyback authorization of about $227 billion by the end of fiscal 2028, as management has said it will, which would shrink the share count. Assuming a net margin of about 50%, TCA's fiscal 2028 EPS estimate lands at $16.12.

Nvidia trades at roughly 10 times forward earnings, far below its historical range. TCA thinks a multiple in the low 20s, near the sector median, would be reasonable. The investor also sees an upside that the model leaves out for now. SpaceX caught Starship's upper stage for the first time last weekend, and TCA thinks cheaper launches could eventually create demand for AI hardware and data centers in space.

title: This Is Incredible News for AMD Stock Investors (Hint: It’s Bad News for Intel)

This Is Incredible News for AMD Stock Investors (Hint: It’s Bad News for Intel)

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) has been crushing Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) in the central processing unit (CPU) market, which explains why the former has been enjoying significantly stronger growth in recent quarters.

In fact, AMD is all set to become a bigger company than Intel in terms of revenue in the current quarter, and a closer look at the developments in the CPU market will tell us just why that's the case. Mercury Research, which provides data on the CPU market, recently released its third-quarter findings, which point to further gains for AMD in a lucrative space.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Let's take a closer look.

Image source: AMD.

AMD is becoming bigger in server CPUs

Server CPU demand has been increasing phenomenally owing to the growth in inference and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) workloads in data centers. Counterpoint Research points out that the ratio of GPU (graphics processing unit) to CPU in AI data centers has moved from 4:1 to 2:1. What's more, the firm sees a GPU to CPU ratio of 1:1 amid rising demand for agentic AI.

In simpler terms, AI data centers are now using more CPUs per GPU, leading to a phenomenal increase in the total addressable market (TAM) for server CPUs. AMD predicts that server CPU TAM will hit $220 billion in 2030, clocking annual growth of more than 50% through the end of the decade. So, AMD's rising share in this space is good news for investors.

Mercury Research points out that AMD's server CPU market share increased to 35.5% in the third quarter, a significant improvement over the year-ago period's reading of 27.8%. So, Intel lost significant ground in this market, which explains why the growth of its data center and AI (DCAI) segment was much slower than AMD's in Q3.

While AMD posted a 97% year-over-year increase in data center revenue last quarter, Intel reported a 78% increase in this segment. The gap is poised to widen in the current quarter. That's because AMD is anticipating 66% revenue growth in the current quarter to $17 billion. Intel, on the other hand, expects 13% revenue growth in the current quarter to $15.5 billion, at the midpoint of its guidance range. That's slower than the 21% revenue jump Intel delivered in Q3.

AMD can continue hurting Intel in this market

It won't be surprising to see AMD taking more market share from Intel in server CPUs next year, thanks mainly to its sixth-generation server CPUs, codenamed Venice. The company began shipping Venice processors to customers last quarter and expects a significant sales ramp next year. In the words of AMD CEO Lisa Su:

Intel is betting its future on its newest process for making chips, called 18A. Winning outside customers for it would add a new source of sales. On its Oct 29 earnings call, Intel's chief executive said the company was "engaged with a couple of highly strategic customers." The harder question is cash.

From 2022 through 2025, Intel spent more on its factories than its business brought in, four years in a row. That shortfall added up to $44.5 billion. In the first nine months of 2026, the gap closed. Operating cash flow, the cash the business brings in, was $13.2 billion. Capital expenditure, the money spent on factories and equipment, was $10.2 billion.

That left about $3.0 billion of free cash flow, the cash left after factory spending. But the gap is closed for now, not for good. Intel's finance chief expects factory spending in 2027 "to be up strongly". On free cash flow next year, he said: "Probably not a dynamic where we're going to have positive free cash flow next year".

How far has Intel stock fallen since September?

Intel closed at $54.67 on Wednesday, Nov 18. That was down 0.91% on the day. The stock has lost 54.5% since its Sep 30 close of $120.23. Even so, it is still up 48.2% in 2026.

Investing.com — The AI chip trade has unraveled this month. Intel's weak forecast set off a broad semiconductor sell-off, and Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL) had already slid about 22% between the first reports of its $115 billion bid for Lumentum and the deal's announcement. Even Lumentum Holdings (NASDAQ:LITE)—the laser maker supplying the optical links inside AI data centers—has plunged 34.0% over the past month to $551.07, including an 11.8% slide in the past week alone.

The headline growth is what makes Lumentum tempting, but the stock no longer trades on its own results. Analysts forecast 121.5% revenue growth and 130.6% EPS growth, yet Marvell's all-stock agreement pays Lumentum shareholders a fixed 4.5 Marvell shares for each share they own, so every slide in Marvell now lands directly on Lumentum's price. GAAP earnings also remain negative at -7.6 times trailing earnings, and InvestingPro's valuation models rate the stock merely "Fair" at $566.14, just 2.7% above the share price. That leaves dip-buyers taking on Marvell's swings without a valuation cushion of their own.

Knowing when a triple-digit sales growth has not yet reached GAAP earnings is what ProPicks AI is built for. In Tech Titans, InvestingPro's strategy dedicated to high-margin tech leaders, Lumentum didn't make the cut: the strategy refused to chase optical-networking hype without GAAP earnings support, keeping members out of the 34% slide and in profitable semiconductor equipment and foundry leaders instead.

The Laser Supplier AI Cannot Get Enough Of

Lumentum makes its money selling the lasers and optical components that carry data between AI servers, and it sells them into a market where demand has outrun supply. It holds dominant share in indium phosphide lasers and high-speed EMLs, commands 70% to 80% of the pump laser market, and is the only merchant supplier of optical circuit switches with a proven shipping track record. Pump laser shipments surged more than 80% year-over-year, backed by three-year take-or-pay agreements with major hyperscalers.

Fiscal fourth-quarter results showed how much that position now earns. Revenue surged 109% year-over-year and 23% sequentially to $1.01 billion, the eighth straight quarter of growth, while non-GAAP gross margin topped 50% for the first time and non-GAAP operating margin expanded 2,160 basis points to 36.6%. The first quarter of fiscal 2027 then beat estimates, with revenue climbing 136.5% year-over-year to $1.26 billion and EPS of $4.57.

Is Intel a Bargain on Cash Flow?

The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model here looks at what Intel might return to shareholders through future free cash flows and brings those numbers back to today. Intel is currently priced at $54.67, yet the model is built on a recent twelve month free cash flow that was a loss of about $2.4b, then assumes a recovering profile that moves into sizeable positive territory over the coming decade.

Those projected gains reflect expectations that investments in foundry, AI chips and cost cuts convert into much stronger cash generation, so the cash flow story leans heavily on execution rather than current results. The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) projections put Intel's estimated intrinsic value substantially above the current share price. Blue-chip stocks have traditionally appealed to long-term investors because of their established market positions, financial resources, and ability to withstand economic uncertainty. However, the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence has complicated the investment outlook for some of the world's largest technology companies. Businesses that have delivered extraordinary earnings growth are now facing questions about whether their momentum can be sustained as spending on AI infrastructure continues to rise.

The concerns have become particularly relevant in 2026. According to a November 10 Reuters report, Wells Fargo upgraded its outlook on US AI infrastructure companies from negative to neutral after semiconductor stocks declined approximately 38% from their June highs. The brokerage argued that the selloff had improved the sector's risk-reward profile, although uncertainty surrounding future AI spending remained.

READ ALSO: 10 Best Stocks to Buy For Next 10 Years

The longer-term outlook presents a more complicated picture. Reuters reported in July that UBS expected capital expenditure by major hyperscalers to rise 76% in 2026, followed by growth of 25% in 2027 and 6% in 2028. These projections highlight an important distinction between sustained investment in AI and continued acceleration in the rate of that investment.

For investors considering a three-year holding period, the central question is therefore not simply which technology companies can benefit from AI demand today. It is which businesses can convert that demand into sustainable earnings, generate sufficient cash flow, and maintain their competitive positions as technology spending patterns evolve. Marvell Technology closed at $145.54 on Wednesday, Nov 18. That is 54% below its record close of $316.43 on June 4. This is the fifth time since 2000 that the stock has halved. The question now is which past fall this one looks like.

So far, on cash, it looks like 2022, not 2006. Operating cash flow is the cash a business brings in from its daily work. In the quarter to Aug 1, 2026, Marvell's came to $605.5 million. That was 31.2% more than a year earlier.

In 2006, cash was also strong when the price halved. The warning sign was profit, which had already been shrinking. Cash flow turned negative only later. The stock took 14.3 years to get back to its 2006 record. After the 2022 fall it took 2.9 years.

How fast has Marvell fallen this time?

Marvell first closed 50% below its June record 154 days after it. That took 175 days in 2006 and 191 days in 2022.

The broad market fell far less over the same months. The S&P 500 slipped 3.4% from June 4 to Nov 18. The Nasdaq-100 fund QQQ fell 11.0%. Marvell's lowest close was $133.55 on Thursday, Nov 5, 57.8% below its high.
